prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks through asset prices and credit, and so generate credit cycles

statement.case_for: The Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles mechanism is a single, well-defined discovery. Collateral values and borrowing constraints feed back on each other, so a small shock to net worth or productivity becomes a large, persistent fluctuation. This is a conceptual contribution, not just a heavily used tool. It is the base of much modern macro-finance, balance-sheet-channel analysis and financial-stability modelling. Attribution is clean: the 1997 paper has two authors, so a two-name citation captures it without arbitrary exclusions. The idea is nearly thirty years old and has been extended in theory, in quantitative macro and, after 2008, in crisis-era work, so there is no maturity concern. After listening to colleagues, I keep this as my preferred single-part configuration. The B019 opening rankings show broad cross-field agreement on the two originators, with all ten proposals including both Kiyotaki and Moore.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from the 2022 recognition of banks and financial crises. Some members may see the financial-frictions theme as already honoured. Direct empirical identification of the collateral amplification channel is also less tidy than the theory's influence suggests. Finally, a two-name citation leaves out the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator strand, which several colleagues want credited. Separately, B010 has much broader opening support than B019 and a more transparent confirmation record through firm-level data. If the Committee judges the 2022 overlap to be decisive, B010 is the strongest alternative.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B010 first. He argued that heterogeneous-firm trade models changed how the field understands selection, reallocation and the gains from trade, and that they extend well beyond the earlier new-trade-theory prize. He noted that Melitz (2003) is central, with Helpman as a major parallel and extending contributor, and that more than twenty years of firm-level evidence confirm it.
responses.response: I have moved toward this view. I ranked B010 sixth mainly out of concern that Krugman's 2008 prize covers part of the ground. Hassler is right that selection into exporting and reallocation across firms is a separate channel, supported by a large body of firm-level evidence, and I now treat B010 as a serious alternative. I still put B019 first, for two reasons. B019 has a tighter single-mechanism attribution. B010 has real credit disputes with Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Eaton-Kortum, which Hassler himself flags. I also cannot combine the two parts under the three-person cap without dropping one of the names that either part needs. My preference is a judgment between two strong candidates, not a claim that B010 is weaker on merit.

responses.point: Stromberg ranked B019 first and proposed adding Mark Gertler. He argued that the financial accelerator is the other half of the credit-friction paradigm, and that Gertler is the strongest credited name on its monetary-policy and banking extensions.
responses.response: I agree that the accelerator is an important part of the same paradigm, and I treat Gertler's claim as real. I still keep the citation to Kiyotaki and Moore. The accelerator line is closely tied to Bernanke, who was recognised in 2022, and Bernanke is not on this ballot. Crediting Gertler without Bernanke would split an overlapping body of work in an awkward way. The collateral-constraint feedback loop also stands alone as a discovery without the accelerator. Stromberg himself concedes that the credit lines need careful drawing to avoid overlap with 2022. A two-name citation is the least contestable way to do that. If the Committee wants a third name, Gertler is the natural one, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B037 first. He argued that Calvo's pricing, Taylor's contracts and rule, and Woodford's integrated framework are the working core of central-bank analysis, that the ideas have decades of use and critique, and that three names can represent the foundations even though the field is crowded.
responses.response: I accept the influence on policy practice and the maturity. My difficulty is attribution. B037 is a collective synthesis built over decades by Calvo, Taylor, Rotemberg, Woodford, Gali, Gertler, Clarida, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets and Wouters. Any three names omit contributors who are plainly central. The triad of Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is defensible, but it is a choice, and I doubt it would hold as a citation. Krusell's own uncertainty list also notes the open debate on how the framework performed in the 2021-23 inflation. B019 does not have this problem, because the discovery is a single mechanism with two clear originators. I keep B037 as an alternative, not a preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the collateral-constraint mechanism as distinct enough from the 2022 recognition of banks and financial crises, given that several colleagues raised this overlap.
Whether Gertler, and by extension Gilchrist and the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator strand, should share the credit, or whether a two-name citation is the cleaner choice.

Whether the case for B010 on breadth of support and firm-level confirmation should outweigh my preference for B019, which depends on how the Committee weighs a single clean mechanism against a larger body of confirming evidence and a harder precursor-credit question.
How strongly the weaker direct empirical identification of the collateral amplification channel should count against the theory's influence.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any B019 candidate (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist) is apparent from the supplied profile. The profile does record connections to others: a long-running collaboration with Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud, Peter Klenow and Huiyu Li, and frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair), who are also IIES colleagues. Klenow is credited on B013, which I do not propose in this round. Krusell and Hassler are members whose openings I discuss above. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
